title: Drona: Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Drona's death
hook: Karna has one weapon he can use only once, saved for Arjuna, and in the middle of the night he has to decide

segments.voice: Yesterday the race against the sun ended with a false sunset and Jayadratha's death. Your line: the sun is still up. Did you take a real pause? Tonight the fighting doesn't stop at dark. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

Lamps. That's what the field looks like now. The armies are so enraged after Jayadratha's death that they keep fighting into the night, and in Ganguli's telling, lamps are lit on chariots and elephants so the warriors can see one another. Darkness belongs to someone on the Pandava side. Ghatotkacha, Bhima's son by Hidimba, a rakshasa, huge and powerful, and strongest at night. He tears into the Kaurava ranks, and they start to break. Today, the weapon Karna has been saving, and who it finally hits.
screen: `LAMPS ON THE FIELD.` → `GHATOTKACHA, BHIMA'S SON.` → `STRONGEST AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Karna carries a dart called the Shakti, a gift from the god Indra. The text tells how he got it: Indra came to him disguised as a brahmana and asked for his natural armor and earrings, and Karna, who would not refuse such a request, cut them from his body and gave them. In return, Indra gave him this weapon, one that would kill any single enemy, but could be used only once. Karna has kept it for Arjuna. Every night he's thought about it. Now the Kauravas are being torn apart by Ghatotkacha, and they beg Karna. Use it, Duryodhana pleads. Or none of us will see morning. Karna hesitates, and then he throws. The Shakti strikes Ghatotkacha, and as he falls, the text says, he makes his body enormous, so that even in dying he crushes part of the Kaurava army beneath him. The Pandavas weep for Bhima's son. And Krishna does something that shocks them. He rejoices. He embraces Arjuna. Arjuna asks how he can be glad at a time like this. Krishna explains. The dart that would have killed you is gone now. Karna has spent it. You are safe from it. A son of the Pandava house has given his life, and in doing it he has drawn off the blow meant for his uncle. The epic holds both at once: real grief for Ghatotkacha, and Krishna's relief, and it won't let either cancel the other.
screen: `THE SHAKTI, USED ONCE` · `"USE IT, OR NONE OF US SEE MORNING"` · `GHATOTKACHA FALLS` · then, large: `KRISHNA REJOICES`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your hands open on your lap. Think of something you've been saving, money, energy, a hard conversation, for one particular moment. Breathe in, and hold it in mind. Breathe out, and ask honestly whether you're keeping it for the right moment, or just keeping it. You don't have to decide. Just look. If you pray, you can name what you are keeping in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Drona. His army fights on into the night, and Karna spends the one weapon he meant for Arjuna.
Your line: has given his life. Today, notice one thing you're saving, and ask whether the moment you're saving it for will ever come. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Ghatotkacha is remembered in Hindu storytelling, and in some regional traditions, as Bhima's loyal son; his night battle and death are told in the Drona Parva of the Mahabharata.

fork.setup: you're Karna. you hold a weapon you can use only once, kept for Arjuna. tonight Ghatotkacha is breaking your army, and Duryodhana is begging. what do you do?
options: keep the dart for Arjuna and fight on without it.
leave the night battle to others.
fork.reveal: Karna throws it. Ghatotkacha falls, and the weapon meant for Arjuna is gone, which is why Krishna rejoices.

original.note: Bhima's son by Hidimba, the rakshasa warrior of the night battle.

trapdoor: what you thought: Krishna was cold about Ghatotkacha's death.
what it means: he was relieved that the dart meant for Arjuna was spent.
what a scholar hears: Ghatotkacha's death is tied to Karna's old gift of his armor and earrings: the bargain with Indra comes due here.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli the lamps lit for the night battle, Ghatotkacha's strength at night, and his enlarging his body as he falls (the number of troops crushed is left out).
Confirm Indra's terms for the Shakti (kills one enemy, usable once) and that Karna had kept it for Arjuna.
Confirm Krishna's rejoicing and explanation; Ganguli's Krishna gives further reasons (e.g., about Ghatotkacha) that are left out.
Editor: 'who never refused a request' narrowed to Indra coming as a brahmana and Karna not refusing such a request.
The earlier wording paraphrased the Vana Parva framing of his generosity; a Keeper may prefer softer wording.
